summary:
Virginia operates within the federal framework of the United States, and the national layer of exposure is carried in the country assessment. State law protects gender identity across several areas a visitor encounters directly, while the state's transgender-related restrictions are concentrated in schools and in rules covering minors.

The Virginia Values Act, passed 6 February 2020, signed 11 April 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit. It covers sexual orientation on the same terms and replaced earlier protections limited to state employment. A law signed 4 March 2020 with the same effective date authorises localities to enact their own sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections.

Violence motivated by gender identity falls within Virginia's hate crime law under legislation signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, which also added sexual orientation. HB 2132, repealing the gay and trans panic defence, passed in March 2021, was signed by Governor Northam, and took effect on 1 July 2021.

State identity documents are comparatively accessible. Virginia has offered an X gender marker on driver's licences since 1 July 2020, and since 1 September 2020 changing the sex designation on a birth certificate requires only "appropriate clinical treatment", replacing a surgery requirement that had been in force since 1979.

The state's criminal provisions on private sexual conduct no longer stand. §18.2-361 was struck down on 12 March 2013 and revised to remove the criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations, by a Senate vote of 40-0 on 7 February 2014 and a House vote of 100-0 on 6 March 2014, signed into immediate effect. §18.2-345 on lewd cohabitation was repealed in 2013 and §18.2-344 on fornication was repealed on 4 March 2020. The sodomy statutes had already been rendered unenforceable by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003.

Marriage between people of the same sex is recognised in Virginia and has been performed since 6 October 2014, when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer and marriages began at 1 p.m. that day. The statutory ban was repealed on 3 March 2020, and a codifying protection was signed in March 2024, effective 1 July. The 2006 constitutional amendment banning such marriages remains in the constitution, with repeal resolutions approved in January 2025 and January 2026 awaiting a voter referendum. A designated-visitor statute signed 26 March 2007 and effective 1 July 2007 extended hospital visitation rights to same-sex couples.

On schools, in 2014 a Gloucester County school board was held to have acted unlawfully in denying a transgender high school student use of the boys' bathroom, a ruling the U.S. Supreme Court allowed to stand in 2021. In July 2023 the state Department of Education adopted policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender students, which were intended to be reversed in 2026. The Virginia High School League barred transgender athletes from girls' sports in February 2025. Virginia prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of minors.

Official posture toward transgender students has moved in both directions through the courts. In September 2021 the Virginia Supreme Court upheld the reinstatement of a teacher suspended for speaking against transgender children and declining to use their pronouns on grounds of Christian belief. In May 2024 Governor Youngkin vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places Virginia in its Low-Risk States group alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, and names Virginia and Arizona as states that have enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on that assessment's reading of state-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.
tangentialFactors:
The state-level document position does not align with the federal travel-document position described at country level: a visitor may hold a Virginia driver's licence or birth certificate carrying markers that the federal passport regime no longer issues, and the two layers have to be read separately.

Virginia's protections for gender identity were enacted by statute in 2020 and by the panic-defence repeal in 2021. Its restrictions on transgender students, by contrast, were adopted administratively by the Department of Education in July 2023 and by the Virginia High School League in February 2025, and the school policies were intended for reversal in 2026.
localsOnly:
Family formation rules matter mainly to residents. Single people may adopt in Virginia with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples adopting, but HB 189 and SB 349, signed 9 April 2012 and effective 1 July 2012, authorise adoption agencies to refuse on religious grounds. A bill passed in February 2019, signed in March 2019 and effective 1 July 2019 legalised surrogacy contracts for same-sex couples, and a February 2021 bill barred taxpayer funds from going to religious organisations that discriminate in adoption.

Health-related provisions affecting residents include the prohibition on providers attempting to change the sexual orientation of minors, alongside the ban on attempts to change a minor's gender identity, and SB 1138, signed 31 March 2021, which decriminalised and modernised Virginia's HIV laws. A bill barring insurance discrimination against PrEP users was vetoed in March 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
A state-by-state list of bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity is attributed in the research to a Movement Advancement Project equality map, but the URL cited for it now returns HTTP 404 after the page moved, and the list could not be verified at the cited address.

Several points remain unresolved. Whether the July 2023 Department of Education policies have in fact been reversed is not established in the available sources. Removal of the 2006 constitutional marriage ban depends on a voter referendum for which no date is sourced. The conclusion that Virginia's youth-targeting policies are unlikely to extend to adults is a risk assessment based on state-specific factors, not a court ruling. No Virginia-specific figures on hate-crime enforcement or on violence against transgender people appear in the available sources.
